arguments.heading: Argument analysis: April 22, 2026 session
paragraphs: This session covered both sides' positions and the questions tested in it. [official source] The government's side tested whether proof duties apply at the border or only later in removal proceedings. [official source] Mr. Lau's side tested whether parole can come before an admissibility determination. [official source]

The government's lawyer conceded the proof standard is not in the statute. [official source] He conceded no constitutional right favors deportable treatment. [official source] He acknowledged the standard usually fails at the border. [official source] He answered that parole does not alter LPR status. [official source]

Mr. Lau's lawyer requested affirmance on a narrow ground or dismissal. [official source] The the opposing side's counsel also requested affirmance or dismissal as improvidently granted. [official source] The government's lawyer disputed the characterization of its parole position. [official source] He answered that a determination precedes parole eligibility but rests on less proof. [official source]

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case is about a green card holder facing removal from the country. [official source] The fight is over which legal box he falls into and how strong the government's proof must be. [official source] One box, called inadmissible, applies at the border. The other, called deportable, applies to people already living here lawfully. [official source]

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The case reached the Supreme Court after earlier rounds of proceedings below. [official source] The Court heard arguments on April 22, 2026, starting at 10:13 in the morning. [official source] Sopan Joshi argued for the federal government. Shay Dvoretzky argued for Mr. Lau. [official source]

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 1, lines 1-9

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Mr. Lau's side asks the Court to either affirm on a narrow timing point or dismiss the case as improvidently granted. [official source] That dismissal request means the Court would drop the case without deciding it. [official source] The government's side asks the Court to rule that the government met its proof duty in the removal proceeding. [official source]

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 40, lines 7-19
Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 73, lines 43-9

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The government's lawyer conceded the tough proof standard does not come from the immigration statute itself. It comes from a Board decision, and the government accepts it here. [official source] The lawyer also said no proof standard is prescribed at the border. If one is needed, it should be a simple satisfaction-of-the-officer test. [official source]

The government's lawyer said the border officer relied on a federal database showing an arrest and a pending charge. [official source] He argued the government must prove, and did prove, by clear and convincing evidence that Mr. Lau was seeking admission at the relevant time. [official source] He also conceded there is no constitutional right to be treated as deportable rather than inadmissible. [official source]

The government's lawyer acknowledged that at border inspection the government usually would not have clear and convincing proof of someone seeking admission. [official source] He said parole does not change lawful permanent resident status. [official source] He acknowledged parole keeps removal open on both inadmissibility and deportability grounds. [official source]

Mr. Lau's lawyer argued the government cannot parole a green card holder just to decide parole eligibility later. Any admissibility exception must be determined first. [official source] He described practical harms: a green card taken and replaced by a one-year stamp, delays in starting removal, job insecurity, and ID worries. He called it a loss of liberty. [official source]

The government's lawyer disputed a claim that the government had said it could parole someone to defer a parole decision. He said they never said that and pointed to their opening brief. [official source] On rebuttal he said there is no evidentiary requirement at the border. The government may meet its burden later in the removal proceeding. [official source]

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: The proof standard matters because clear and convincing proof is very hard to meet. [official source] The government's own lawyer admitted that standard usually cannot be met at the border itself. [official source] So the timing question decides where and when the government must build its case. [official source]

The outcome also affects real people facing removal. Mr. Lau's lawyer described lost green cards, one-year stamps, job insecurity, and delays. [official source] Both sides agreed parole does not erase lawful permanent resident status. [official source]
